So, two weeks. Where have you been so far, and what was the worst part?
Florence, three days. The worst part was August. The centre was packed, and we spent more time in queues than in front of anything.
Everybody makes that mistake. Nobody tells you to leave. Did you go anywhere off the beaten track?
One day trip, to Lucca. Fifty minutes on the train, and it was far quieter than anywhere else we had been.
And? Better than Florence?

Not better. Nowhere near as impressive, honestly. But we walked the whole wall in an hour, we had lunch in a place with six tables, and it was by far the best meal of the trip. It was worth the detour.
That is the right answer. Where are you going next, and how long do you have?
Four days here, then a stopover in Lisbon on the way home. What would you do with four days, if you had never seen the city?

I stopped making lists about six years ago and it is the best decision I have made as a traveller. Not because lists are wrong, but because a list turns a city into a series of tasks, and you spend the whole afternoon walking past the thing you would have loved on your way to the thing somebody told you to see. Now I do one thing in the morning, properly, and then I wander until I am tired. The result is that I remember far less and far better. Ask me about the most famous church in a city I visited last year and I probably cannot tell you much. Ask me about the street I got lost in and I can describe the light. The other thing I have learned is that the second city is almost always more interesting than the first. Everybody goes to the obvious one, and the town forty minutes away is quieter, cheaper and about eighty per cent as good, which is a much better deal than it sounds.

The best day of that whole trip was not planned at all. We had three days in Florence, which is two days more than we needed, if I am honest, because in August the centre is packed and you spend more time in queues than in front of anything. So on the second morning we took a train to Lucca, which is fifty minutes away and which almost nobody had mentioned to us. It is a small walled town, you can walk the entire wall in an hour, and the whole place was noticeably calmer than where we had come from. We had lunch in a place with six tables, and it was easily the best meal of the two weeks. The point is not that Lucca is better than Florence, because it is not, and I would go back to Florence tomorrow. The point is that the day trip was worth far more to us than a third day of standing in a queue.
